lessons.title: Case: introducing a CV screening tool
lessons.subtitle: Check an AI decision memo against the legal sources

concept.body:
Fictional case: XY GmbH, a machine builder with 200 staff, wants to use a purchased tool that ranks CVs by match score and prepares a shortlist. An AI assistant drafted the decision memo for management.

Check the memo the way a supervisory authority would. Watch for three mix-ups:

- a final human decision taken for the Art. 6(3) exception,
- public-body obligations applied to private deployers,
- provider obligations placed on the deployer.

Alongside the AI Act, German anti-discrimination law (AGG), Art. 22 GDPR for solely automated decisions and works council co-determination under section 87(1) no. 6 BetrVG, where a works council exists, still apply.
concept.takeaway: Every statement in the memo needs an article behind it, or it goes.

exercise.title: Check the decision memo
exercise.instructions: Judge each underlined statement against the five sources as supported, contradicted or not in the sources, then evaluate. Company and tool are fictional.

sources.label: Source A: Annex III point 4(a) AI Act (extract)
sources.text: AI systems intended to be used for the recruitment or selection of natural persons, in particular to place targeted job advertisements, to analyse and filter job applications, and to evaluate candidates.

sources.label: Source B: Art. 6(3) AI Act (shortened)
sources.text: An AI system referred to in Annex III shall not be considered high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk and does not materially influence the outcome of decision making. An AI system referred to in Annex III shall always be considered high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons.

sources.label: Source C: Art. 26 AI Act (summarised)
sources.text: Para. 6: deployers keep automatically generated logs, to the extent they are under their control, for at least six months. Para. 7: deployers who are employers inform workers' representatives and the affected workers before putting the system into service at the workplace.

sources.label: Source D: Art. 27(1) AI Act (summarised)
sources.text: A fundamental rights impact assessment is carried out by bodies governed by public law, private entities providing public services, and deployers of systems under Annex III point 5(b) and (c).

sources.label: Source E: Art. 16 AI Act and timeline (summarised)
sources.text: Providers of high-risk systems carry out the conformity assessment, draw up the EU declaration of conformity and affix the CE marking. Under Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 the high-risk rules for stand-alone Annex III systems apply from 2 December 2027.

props.draftLabel: AI draft: decision memo for management

draft.text: The tool ranks CVs by match score and
therefore falls under Annex III point 4(a)
Because a human always makes the final decision, the Art. 6(3) exception applies
we keep the logs for at least six months
inform the works council and affected staff before use
we carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment under Art. 27 before use
do the conformity assessment and CE marking ourselves
The provider guarantees that the tool is free of discrimination

claims.evidence: to analyse and filter job applications, and to evaluate candidates
claims.why: A match-score ranking analyses, filters and evaluates applications.

claims.evidence: An AI system referred to in Annex III shall always be considered high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons.
claims.correction: The exception does not apply: the match score evaluates people (profiling) and decides whom humans see at all.
claims.why: A final human decision is not the Art. 6(3) exception.
Art. 26(6), to the extent the logs are under the deployer's control.

claims.evidence: inform workers' representatives and the affected workers before putting the system into service at the workplace
claims.why: Art. 26(7). Co-determination rights under German labour law come on top.

claims.evidence: A fundamental rights impact assessment is carried out by bodies governed by public law, private entities providing public services, and deployers of systems under Annex III point 5(b) and (c).
claims.correction: Art. 27 does not require a fundamental rights impact assessment here. Whether the GDPR requires a data protection impact assessment is a separate check.
claims.why: A private employer using Annex III point 4 is not an addressee.

claims.evidence: Providers of high-risk systems carry out the conformity assessment, draw up the EU declaration of conformity and affix the CE marking.
claims.correction: That is a provider duty. XY GmbH checks documents, marking and instructions for use, as long as no role flip under Art. 25 occurs.
claims.why: Provider and deployer duties are mixed up.

claims.correction: Delete it. Request bias tests and documents from the provider; anti-discrimination law applies regardless.
claims.why: No source supports such a guarantee.

claims.evidence: the high-risk rules for stand-alone Annex III systems apply from 2 December 2027

checks.prompt: XY GmbH retrains the tool on its own data, substantially modifies it and markets it to partner firms under its own name. What changes?

options.feedback: Its own name and a substantial modification of a high-risk system trigger Art. 25.
Distributors pass a system on unchanged under someone else's name.

options.text: It becomes the provider under Art. 25 and carries conformity assessment and technical documentation

checks.explanation: With the role flip, the provider obligations under Art. 16 apply to it for this system.

checks.prompt: When do you also check Art. 22 GDPR?

options.text: Never; the AI Act displaces the GDPR
options.feedback: Art. 2(7) AI Act leaves the GDPR unaffected.

options.text: When a solely automated decision with legal or similarly significant effects could be involved

options.feedback: Art. 22 GDPR attaches to automated decisions, not to a data category.

checks.explanation: A merely formal click by a human does not reliably remove the 'solely automated' element. Check the exception and the safeguards.

lessons.title: Your inventory entry and 30-day plan
lessons.subtitle: Role, class, obligations and deadline in one document

concept.body:
An inventory is your most important working tool: it shows which systems run, for what, in which role and with which class. The Regulation prescribes no format for deployers, and a spreadsheet alone does not prove compliance.

Useful fields per system: name and version, function actually used, role, risk class with reasoning, obligations and deadline, owner, provider documents, next review trigger.

Then a 30-day plan: find shadow AI through procurement, invoices and SSO approvals, classify every system, assign owners and deadlines to every gap, document Art. 4 measures.

Reclassify after substantial changes to system, purpose, provider or data, after incidents and after changes in law.
concept.takeaway: One entry per system, with reasoning and an owner, and a plan with deadlines.

exercise.title: Create your first inventory entry
exercise.instructions: Fill in the required fields for one system from your work, for example the CV tool from the case. The preview shows the finished document; download it as Markdown or copy it.

fields.label: Purpose and function used
fields.placeholder: Ranks incoming applications by match score for shortlisting

fields.label: Reasoning for the class
fields.placeholder: Analyses and evaluates applications (Annex III point 4(a)); profiling, so no exception

fields.label: Obligations
options: Logs for at least six months (Art. 26(6))

fields.label: 30-day plan
options: Week 1: find shadow AI through procurement, invoices and SSO approvals
Week 2: classify every system by role and class
Week 3: assign owners and deadlines to every gap
Week 4: document Art. 4 measures and request provider documents

fields.label: Next review trigger
fields.placeholder: New version, change of purpose, incident or change in law

checks.prompt: Does the AI Act prescribe a specific inventory format for deployers?

options.feedback: No such mandatory template exists for deployers.

options.text: No; what matters is that role, purpose, class and obligations are traceably documented
Yes, a form for high-risk systems
options.feedback: Even for high-risk systems there is no mandatory form for private deployers. Providers register in the EU database under Art. 49.

checks.explanation: The inventory is a working tool for your evidence. Pick a tool in which ownership, access rights and changes stay manageable.

checks.prompt: When do you reclassify a system?

options.feedback: Updates, new purposes and changes in law can change the class.
By then it is too late. The classification must be right beforehand.

options.text: After substantial changes to system, purpose, provider or data, after incidents and after changes in law

checks.explanation: A substantial modification can end transition rules; a change of purpose can change the class or even the role.
